warmup.q: The payments app keeps idle connections in its pool for 10 minutes. The load balancer in front of the bank forgets idle connections after 350 seconds, without telling anyone. After a quiet 6 minutes, what happens to the next payment request?
options: It works: the pool checks each connection before using it
It gets a reset and fails, before any of the bank's machines has seen it
It waits until the connect timeout runs out
The load balancer answers with an HTTP error saying the request took too long
warmup.why: The pool still lists the connection as idle and healthy, because the balancer forgot it without telling anyone. The request goes out on it, and the balancer, which has no record of the connection, answers with a TCP reset: TCP's way of saying "I don't know this connection". The AWS documentation describes exactly this for its network load balancer. None of the bank's machines saw the request. Java's HTTP client would quietly retry a GET in this case, but not a POST. That's the café's Monday morning, and the last section shows the fix: the pool's idle timeout must be shorter than the balancer's.

sections.h: One address, many servers: a load balancer turns one request into two connections
sections.html:
The bank runs its payment program on 20 machines, but the payments app knows one name. Something has to spread the app's requests over those machines, and stop sending to the one that has crashed. DNS can hand out several addresses (lesson 9 of this track, DNS: how a name becomes an address). But every copy of a DNS answer is kept until it expires, so a dead machine stays in use until all the copies run out. So almost every busy service sits behind a load balancer: one address that accepts connections and passes the work to a healthy backend, one of the machines behind it.

Think of the front desk of a big office. A mail room reads the address on each envelope and drops it in the right tray, unopened. A receptionist opens each letter, reads it, and writes a fresh one to the right department. Load balancers come in the same two kinds. Network people number the layers of the stack. Layer 4 is the transport, where TCP lives (the protocol that carries a stream of bytes between two programs). Layer 7 is the application, where HTTP lives (the protocol of web requests).

The mail-room kind is an L4 load balancer. It picks a backend when a connection opens, in turn or by a hash (a number worked out from the addresses and the ports, the numbers that pick out each program). From then on it copies bytes both ways without reading them. Some rewrite the addresses on packets, like the NAT of lesson 3 (a box that rewrites addresses), so the backend sees the app's address. Others, like Lb.java in the Try it, accept the app's TCP connection and open a second one of their own to the backend. A program that sits in the middle like this, taking one connection and opening its own, is called a proxy. Either way, an L4 balancer spreads connections, not requests. An app with a pool of four long-lived connections sends all its traffic to at most four backends, however many there are.

The receptionist kind is an L7 load balancer. It ends the app's TCP connection and its TLS, the locking from lesson 10 (so it holds the certificate), reads each HTTP request, and picks a backend for each one. It can send /authorize and /refunds to different groups of machines. Then it forwards the request over its own pooled connections. AWS, Amazon's cloud service, describes its L7 balancer exactly so: it keeps "one connection with the client and one connection with a target".

Two connections mean the backend no longer sees the app. In the Try it, both backends log every request as coming from 10.10.2.2, the balancer. An L7 balancer passes the app's address on in the X-Forwarded-For header, an extra line in the request (or in the standard Forwarded header, from RFC 7239, the public document that defines it). An L4 proxy can put a PROXY protocol header in front of the bytes instead. Read X-Forwarded-For with care. A client can send its own, and the balancer only adds to the end of it, so in the Try it a forged 203.0.113.7 arrives ahead of the real address. Trust only the entries your own proxies added, counting from the right.

A balancer also checks its backends. It sends a small request every few seconds, and stops routing to a backend that fails several in a row. When a backend is about to be replaced, the balancer drains it: no new requests, while those in flight may finish. The balancer decides where a request goes. Next, we'll decide how long the app should wait for the answer.

try.title: Watch an L4 and an L7 balancer forward the same request
steps: Work from the labs folder, with the lab network up: docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d. It's a small pretend network of containers, programs that each behave like a separate small computer. The commands start two backends on server: Backend.java on ports 8081 and 8082. Each answers with its name, the address the request came from, and the X-Forwarded-For header. They also start two balancers on router: Lb.java l4 on port 8080 and Lb.java l7 on 8090. The two until lines wait for the four Java programs to start.
client then sends two requests through each balancer, and one more through the L7 one with a forged X-Forwarded-For. Predict: which address does each backend see, and what's in the header?
The last lines list router's TCP connections with ss, a tool that shows connections, then stop the Java programs.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: n() { docker compose -f env/net.yml exec "$@"; } D=/labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l12/demo n -d server sh -c "java $D/Backend.java 8081 ledger-a > /tmp/a.log" n -d server sh -c "java $D/Backend.java 8082 ledger-b > /tmp/b.log" n -d router sh -c "java $D/Lb.java l4 8080 10.10.2.20:8081,10.10.2.20:8082 > /tmp/l4.log" n -d router sh -c "java $D/Lb.java l7 8090 10.10.2.20:8081,10.10.2.20:8082 > /tmp/l7.log" n router sh -c 'until grep -q L4 /tmp/l4.log && grep -q L7 /tmp/l7.log; do sleep 0.5; done' n server sh -c 'until grep -q listening /tmp/a.log && grep -q listening /tmp/b.log; do sleep 0.5; done' n client sh -c 'for i in 1 2; do curl -s http://10.10.1.2:8080/authorize; done' n client sh -c 'for i in 1 2; do curl -s http://10.10.1.2:8090/authorize; done' n client curl -s -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7' http://10.10.1.2:8090/authorize n router ss -tn n router pkill java; n server pkill java

try.expect:
From one run:

ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55358, X-Forwarded-For: (none)
ledger-b GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:56946, X-Forwarded-For: (none)
ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55362, X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10
ledger-b GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:56954, X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10
ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55362, X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, 10.10.1.10
State Recv-Q Send-Q      Local Address:Port         Peer Address:PortProcess
ESTAB 0      0      [::ffff:10.10.2.2]:55362 [::ffff:10.10.2.20]:8081
ESTAB 0      0      [::ffff:10.10.2.2]:56954 [::ffff:10.10.2.20]:8082

Through either balancer, the backends see 10.10.2.2, router's address on the server's network, and never client's 10.10.1.10: each request travelled over two TCP connections. Both balancers took turns between the backends. Only the L7 one, which reads the HTTP request, could add X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10. It added the real address after the forged 203.0.113.7, so the rightmost entry is the one to trust. The last request reused local port 55362. The L7 balancer keeps its own pool of connections to the backends, and those two are still open, while the L4 connections closed with their clients. Your port numbers will differ.

sections.h: How long to wait: one timeout is not enough
sections.html:
Lesson 7 of this track, TCP connections, timed a connect to a computer behind a firewall (a box that filters traffic) that silently drops packets. Linux, the operating system in the lab, resends the first message of the handshake, the exchange that opens a connection (that message is the SYN). It gives up after about 136 seconds. A thread, one line of work inside a program, that waits 136 seconds for one payment serves nobody else in that time. A pool of 20 connections all stuck like that is an app that has stopped. Every call over the network needs a limit on how long it may wait, called a timeout. The question is: wait for what?

One call to the bank waits for several things, one after another:

  1. a free connection from the pool, if they're all busy;
  2. DNS, if the name's address isn't saved yet (lesson 9);
  3. the TCP handshake, one round trip there and back (lesson 7);
  4. the TLS handshake, another round trip (lesson 10);
  5. the answer's headers: the bank's own work, 120 ms (thousandths of a second) on a good day;
  6. the answer's body, which may arrive in pieces.

Each one fails for its own reasons, so each deserves its own limit. A connect that takes more than a few round trips won't succeed: the address is wrong, a firewall drops it, or the machine is down. So the connect timeout can be short, a second or two. Waiting for the answer is the bank's work, so that limit comes from how long the bank takes, a little above its slowest normal answers. People measure those with the p99, the time that 99 answers in 100 beat. Waiting for a connection from the pool means the app itself is overloaded. There the right move is to fail within tens of milliseconds, not to join a queue.

The body hides a trap. A read timeout (Socket.setSoTimeout in Java) limits each read, not the whole answer. A server that sends one byte every 500 ms never trips a 1-second read timeout, and a 20-byte body takes 10 seconds. The request timeout of the JDK HttpClient, Java's built-in web client (HttpRequest.Builder.timeout), stops waiting once the answer's headers have arrived, so it doesn't catch this either. Only a deadline on the whole call does: sendAsync(...).orTimeout(...) with the JDK client. The Try it shows all four cases.

The JDK HttpClient has connectTimeout on the client and timeout on each request. Its HTTP/1.1 pool has no size limit, so it never waits for a connection. Pools with a maximum size, such as the one in Apache HttpClient (a popular free Java library), have a separate timeout for that wait, which Apache calls the connection request timeout. Set each one on purpose. And when the app calls another program, pass on the time that's left: a request with 2 seconds left shouldn't start a call that may take 5.

Every wait gets its own limit. The whole call gets a deadline. A timeout tells the app when to give up. Next, we'll ask when it should try again.

try.title: Four calls, four timeouts
steps: In the lab box (docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box, a Linux shell in a container with this track's tools), run Timeouts.java. It starts a badly behaved server of its own on 127.0.0.1, the computer's own address. Then it makes four calls with the JDK HttpClient, all with a 1-second connect timeout and a 1-second request timeout.

Predict how long each call takes before you run it: a connect to an address nobody answers, a server that is silent for 3 s, a server that sends its headers at once and then one byte every 500 ms, and the same with a 2-second deadline on the whole call.
try.expect:
From one run:

1. connect to a silent address           1.1 s  HttpConnectTimeoutException: HTTP connect timed out
2. a server that takes 3 s to answer     1.0 s  HttpTimeoutException: request timed out
3. a body that trickles in              10.3 s  200, 20 bytes of body
4. the same, with a 2 s deadline         2.0 s  TimeoutException: null

The connect timeout caught the silent address after 1 second, instead of Linux's 136. The request timeout caught the silent server. But the third call took 10.3 seconds with the same two timeouts. The headers came at once, which satisfied the request timeout, and the body then crawled in for 10 seconds with nothing left to stop it. Only the deadline on the whole call, orTimeout on the CompletableFuture (Java's object for a result that will arrive later), cut it off at 2 seconds. (null is the JDK's message for that exception.)

sections.h: Trying again: retries help only when they're safe and spread out
sections.html:
A retry turns a failure into a second request. Sometimes that's exactly right. The connection was reset, the backend restarted, and the next attempt lands on a healthy one. Sometimes it's a disaster.

Safety first. Say POST /authorize timed out after the request went out. You don't know whether the bank approved the payment, and sending it again may charge the card twice. RFC 9110, the document that defines HTTP's methods, names the ones that are safe to repeat. A request is idempotent when sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE are. POST isn't, unless the bank accepts an idempotency key: a unique id per payment, which the server stores with the result. A second request with the same key gets the first result back, not a second charge.

So sort failures by what they tell you. A request that never left is always safe to send again: connection refused (nothing was listening at that address) and connect timeout (lesson 7). After a reset or a read timeout, the request may have arrived, so only an idempotent request may go again. A 400 ("bad request") or a 500 ("server error") will come back the same the second time, so don't retry those at all.

Then spread the retries out. Picture 1,000 cafés whose payments all fail at the same moment, because the bank's program restarted. If each one retries after a fixed 100 ms, all 1,000 retries arrive in the same instant. The bank falls over again, and the next round is packed as tightly. Exponential backoff, waiting 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, up to a cap, slows the rounds down. But it keeps them in step, because every client works out the same waits. Full jitter breaks the rhythm: each client waits a random time between zero and the current ceiling. The Try it simulates exactly this case. With jitter, all 1,000 clients are answered within about 1.1 seconds. Without it, 600 of them never are.

Retries also multiply. Say a request passes through three programs, each calling the next, and each one tries 3 times. One request at the top can become 27 at the bottom, at the moment the bottom can least afford them. A retry budget caps the extra load: retries may add at most about 10% to what a client sends, and once that budget is spent, failures go straight back to the caller. Retry at one layer, usually the one closest to the user, and let the others fail fast.

A retry rescues a request that met a broken connection. Next, we'll find where most of those broken connections come from, and solve the café's Monday morning.

try.title: Simulate a retry storm
steps: In the lab box, run Jitter.java. It simulates 1,000 clients whose first request fails, because the bank (the code says issuer, the bank that issued the card) is down until 250 ms. After that, the bank answers at most 100 requests per 10 ms. Every failed client retries with exponential backoff, at most 6 attempts in all.
Predict before you run it: with jitter or without, which gets more clients answered, and which sends more requests in total?
try.expect:
From one run (the numbers are the same every time, because the simulation uses a fixed random seed):

no jitter: wait min(1 s, 100 ms x 2^n)
     ms  arrived  answered
      0     1000         0
    100     1000         0
    300     1000       100
    700      900       100
   1500      800       100
  answered 400 of 1000 clients, the last at 2500 ms; 5400 requests in all; busiest 10 ms: 1000 retries

full jitter: wait random(0, min(1 s, 100 ms x 2^n))
     ms  arrived  answered
      0     2269         0
    100      635         0
    200      488       198
    300      266       266
    400      260       260
    500      138       138
    600       39        39
    700       31        31
    800       42        42
    900       18        18
   1000        6         6
   1100        2         2
  answered 1000 of 1000 clients, the last at 1128 ms; 4194 requests in all; busiest 10 ms: 155 retries

Without jitter, every retry round lands in a single 10 ms slot: 1,000 requests where 100 fit. So 900 fail and come back together, 400 ms later, to fail again. After six attempts 600 clients have given up, and the bank saw 5,400 requests. With full jitter, retries spread out: never more than 155 in any 10 ms, every client answered within 1.13 seconds, and fewer requests in total. The busy first 100 ms with jitter is the original 1,000 requests plus early retries, hitting a bank that is still down. None of them can succeed before 250 ms either way.

aside.title: Why not retry every failure three times, at every layer?
aside.html: It's the first fix many teams reach for, because the first failure they meet is a one-off reset that a retry makes go away. But it charges a card twice when a POST /authorize that timed out had in fact gone through. And during an outage at the bank, it multiplies the load at the very moment the bank tries to recover: three layers of three attempts turn one request into 27. Sort the failure first. Never sent is always safe to retry, maybe processed only for an idempotent request, and a 400 or a 500 never. Then wait with full jitter, keep a retry budget of about 10%, and retry at one layer only.

sections.h: Why the first payment of the morning fails: idle connections and their timers
sections.html:
Remember the café whose first payment of the morning fails? Here's where it starts. A new connection to a bank 70 ms away costs a TCP round trip and a TLS round trip: 140 ms before the request may leave. It also leaves a TIME-WAIT entry, a short wait a closed connection leaves behind, on whichever side closes first (lesson 7). A connection pool keeps connections open between requests, so only the first request pays. Three different things are all called "keepalive", and they're easy to mix up:

  • HTTP keep-alive is reuse: HTTP/1.1's connections that stay open (the last lesson), which make a pool possible.
  • TCP keepalive (SO_KEEPALIVE) sends empty probes on an idle connection to check that the other end is still there. On Linux the first probe goes out after 2 hours of silence.
  • Protocol pings, such as HTTP/2's PING frame (a small message) or gRPC's keepalive, do the same job inside the program's own protocol. (gRPC is a popular way for programs to call each other over HTTP/2.)

Every hop on the path keeps idle connections for a while and then forgets them, each by its own clock. The JDK's HttpClient keeps an idle connection for 30 seconds (jdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout), and the JDK's HttpServer closes one after 30 seconds (sun.net.httpserver.idleInterval). AWS's application load balancer, its L7 kind, closes connections that have been idle for 60 seconds. Its network load balancer, the L4 kind, stops tracking a connection after 350 seconds. If data arrives later, the AWS documentation says, "the client receives a TCP RST packet": a reset, TCP's way of saying "I don't know this connection". The NAT gateways of lesson 3, boxes that share one address among many computers, behave the same way at 350 seconds.

Now the mystery. The café's payments app keeps idle connections in its pool for 10 minutes. A network load balancer in front of the bank forgets them after 350 seconds, and tells nobody. The café is quiet overnight. In the morning, the first payment goes out on a pooled connection the balancer no longer knows. The balancer answers with a reset, and the payment fails before any of the bank's machines has seen it. The cashier taps again, the pool opens a fresh connection, and that works. It looks random: only the first call after a quiet spell fails, and never under load, which is when people test.

In the front-desk picture, the receptionist threw away the file on a conversation that had gone quiet, and when you call back about it, she has no idea what you mean. The picture breaks here. She would ask you to start again, while the balancer hangs up and leaves the app to guess whether its request ever arrived.

The fix follows from the picture. Each client's idle timeout must be shorter than the next hop's. The pool's must be below the load balancer's, and the load balancer's below the backend's, which is what AWS recommends for its own balancer. Add a maximum connection lifetime, so that connections also follow changes in DNS (lesson 9). And retry an idempotent request once, straight away, when a reused connection is reset before any answer. The JDK client already does that for GET, which is why the GET in the Try it survives the reset and the POST does not.

All of this lowers the odds of a failed payment. It can't bring them to zero: a request that was sent and got no answer still leaves the app not knowing what happened.

stepper.title: A timeout, a retry and an idle connection that turns into a reset

The ceiling was 100 ms and jitter picked 37.</text></svg>
frames.say: A GET is idempotent, so the app may try again. It waits a random time between 0 and the current ceiling of 100 ms (full jitter), 37 ms this time, so that a thousand clients that failed together don't come back together. The new connection lands on ledger-b, which answers 200.

frames.say: Five seconds of silence. The balancer drops connection 2 from its table and closes its own connection to ledger-b. It sends nothing to the app, as cloud network load balancers and NAT gateways do. The pool still lists connection 2 as idle and healthy.

frames.say: The next payment takes the idle connection from the pool. The balancer has no record of it, and answers with a reset. No backend ever saw the request, but the app can't know that, and a POST without an idempotency key must not be sent again blindly. The JDK quietly retries a GET in this situation. The POST fails.

frames.say: The fix is a rule: each client's idle timeout must be shorter than the next hop's. With the pool's set to 4 seconds, the pool closes connection 2 at 5.1 s, before the balancer forgets it. The POST at 9 s opens a fresh connection and gets its 200. The Try it below runs both versions.

try.title: Reproduce the idle-timeout reset
steps: In the lab box, start one backend and an L4 balancer that forgets connections after 5 seconds of silence and resets them on their next use, like a cloud network load balancer. tcpdump, a program that records packets, notes every reset on port 8080.

Caller.java plays the payments app, with one long-lived JDK HttpClient. It sends a request at once, another 2 s later, and a third 9 s after the start, 7 s after the second. Predict what happens to the third call as a POST, as a GET, and as a POST with the pool's idle timeout set to 4 s.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: D=/labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l12/demo java $D/Backend.java 8081 ledger-a > /tmp/b.log & java $D/Lb.java l4 8080 127.0.0.1:8081 5 > /tmp/lb.log & until grep -q listening /tmp/b.log 2>/dev/null && grep -q L4 /tmp/lb.log 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.2; done tcpdump -i lo -nn --immediate-mode -w /tmp/rst.pcap 'tcp port 8080 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' 2>/dev/null & java $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/authorize POST 0,2,9 java $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/payments/42 GET 0,2,9 java -Djdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout=4 $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/authorize POST 0,2,9 kill %3; wait %3 2>/dev/null grep -E 'forgotten|reset' /tmp/lb.log tcpdump -r /tmp/rst.pcap -nn 2>/dev/null

try.expect:
From one run (the backend's reply after 200 trimmed, and tcpdump's options too):

pool idle timeout: 30 (the default) s
22:06:34  t= 0.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:34980, ...
22:06:36  t= 2.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:34980, ...
22:06:43  t= 9.0 s  POST  failed: IOException: HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes (SocketException: Connection reset)
pool idle timeout: 30 (the default) s
22:06:47  t= 0.1 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:56602, ...
22:06:49  t= 2.0 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:56602, ...
22:06:56  t= 9.0 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:41334, ...
pool idle timeout: 4 s
22:07:02  t= 0.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:51934, ...
22:07:04  t= 2.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:51934, ...
22:07:11  t= 9.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:50176, ...
22:06:41  lb: connection 1: idle for 5 s, forgotten (backend side closed, client not told)
22:06:43  lb: connection 1: data after the idle timeout, sending a reset
22:06:54  lb: connection 2: idle for 5 s, forgotten (backend side closed, client not told)
22:06:56  lb: connection 2: data after the idle timeout, sending a reset
22:06:43.380409 IP 127.0.0.1.8080 > 127.0.0.1.43998: Flags [R.], seq 454177905, ack 4048227309, win 512, length 0
22:06:56.417297 IP 127.0.0.1.8080 > 127.0.0.1.42254: Flags [R.], seq 814232598, ack 941334079, win 512, length 0

The first two calls of each run share a connection: the backend sees the same port. At 9 s, the POST went out on a connection the balancer had forgotten 2 seconds earlier, and the reset came back. That's the first RST in the capture, and the JDK's confusing "header parser received no bytes". The GET met the same reset (the second RST), but the JDK quietly retried it on a new connection, which is why the backend saw a new port, 41334. The JDK does that only for requests it considers idempotent. With the pool's idle timeout at 4 s, the pool closed the connection before the balancer forgot it, and the third POST opened a new one without any fuss. Your times and ports will differ.

refs.title: AWS: Network Load Balancers (connection idle timeout)

opening:
Picture a café on a Monday morning. The first customer taps a card, and the reader shows an error. The cashier asks them to tap again, and this time it works. All day, every payment goes through. On Tuesday morning, the same thing happens: the first payment fails, and the second works.

It's tempting to call the network flaky and make the app try every failed payment again. Careful teams do exactly that, because a retry makes the error go away. But a payment sent twice can charge a card twice, and a thousand apps retrying at once can knock a bank over.

The last lesson, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over QUIC, showed how one connection carries many requests. In this lesson, we'll follow a payment through what sits between the app and the bank. We'll meet a load balancer that spreads the work, timeouts, retries, and a pool of connections kept open for reuse. By the end, we'll know why the first payment of the morning fails. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café whose first card payment of every morning failed. Two clocks disagreed: the app's pool kept a quiet connection for 10 minutes, and the load balancer forgot it after 350 seconds.

After a minute of browsing, run netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED in a terminal on a Mac or Linux computer. Each line is a connection your browser keeps open to reuse. Stop browsing for a few minutes, run it again, and see which have gone.

Every connection, timer and resend in this track was run by the kernel, the core of the operating system. Next, in the Operating systems track, we'll ask what a kernel is, and why a program must ask it before it can send a single byte.

compare.note: Both come from the last Try it. The only change is -Djdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout=4. When the client gives up on an idle connection first, the worst that can happen is a new handshake. When the balancer gives up first, the next request on that connection is lost. Set every client's idle timeout below the next hop's, all the way down the path.

worked.title: Choose the timeouts and the pool for one issuer call

steps.say: Start from measurements, not defaults. Suppose the bank (the issuer, in the code: the bank that issued the card) is 70 ms away. It answers in 120 ms on average, and in 400 ms at the p99, the time 99 answers in 100 beat. The app's own checkout promises its callers an answer within 2 seconds. At the busiest time, 200 payments arrive every second.
steps.code:
round trip           70 ms
issuer p50 / p99     120 ms / 400 ms
our own deadline     2 s for the whole checkout call
peak load            200 authorizations / s

steps.say: Size the pool with Little's law: requests in flight = arrival rate x the time each one takes. At the average, that's 24 connections busy at once. Give it room for slow spells, because when the bank slows down, more requests overlap.
steps.code:
200 / s x 0.12 s = 24 in flight on average
200 / s x 0.40 s = 80 if every call took the p99
pool: 40 connections; wait at most 50 ms for one, then fail fast

steps.say: Connect timeout: a handshake takes one round trip, 70 ms. Linux resends a lost SYN, the first handshake message, after 1 second (lesson 7), so 1.5 s lets one resend through and still fails fast on a dead address. Response timeout: twice the p99. Deadline: whatever is left of the caller's 2 seconds, so one retry of 800 ms plus its wait still fits.
steps.code:
connect timeout      1.5 s     one SYN resend fits
response timeout     800 ms    2 x p99, until the headers
deadline             2 s       the whole call, body and one retry included
retry                1, only with the Idempotency-Key, after random(0, 100 ms)

steps.say: Idle timeouts: the pool's below the balancer's, and the balancer's below the backend's. Then write it all down in code. The JDK client takes the pool's idle timeout as a system property, a setting given on the command line.
steps.code: // -Djdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout=30 (pool idle 30 s < balancer 60 s < backend 75 s) val client: HttpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder() .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(1_500)) // one SYN resend fits .build() fun authorize(json: String, key: String): HttpResponse<String> { val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.issuer.example/authorize")) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(800)) // until the response headers .header("Idempotency-Key", key) // makes one retry safe .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json)) .build() return client.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // the deadline: body included .join() }

lab.title: A retry policy and a connection pool against a load balancer that forgets
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 17 fail. Http.kt (requests, outcomes and the Connection interface) and Caller.kt (one call: take a connection, send, give it back, ask the policy) are finished. The tests use FakeLb from the test folder: a load balancer that forgets connections idle for 350 seconds and resets them on their next use, timed by a ManualClock that the test moves forward by hand.

In RetryPolicy.kt, write RetryBudget first, then isIdempotent, mayRetry, backoffMs (full jitter below a capped exponential ceiling) and decide. RetryPolicyTest passes in a fixed random number, so the waits come out exact.

In ConnectionPool.kt, write acquire and release. Throw out idle connections past the idle timeout or the maximum lifetime, reuse the one released most recently, open a new one while below the maximum size, and throw PoolExhausted above it.

IdleMismatchTest puts it all together: a pool that keeps idle connections for 600 s meets the balancer's 350 s, and then a pool with 300 s does not. Run the tests until all 17 pass, then read the test's log lines next to the stepper.
hints: baseMs shl (retry - 1) doubles the ceiling. Cap the shift (say at 30) so that a large retry number can't overflow, then take min(capMs, ...) and multiply by random().
In decide, check attempts, then mayRetry, and only then budget.tryRetry(): a retry you refuse anyway must not use up a token.
Ten additions of 0.1 make 0.9999999999999999, so compare the budget's tokens with 1.0 - 1e-9, not 1.0.

In the pool, keep id -> openedAt for every open connection, and a deque (a list you can use from both ends) of (connection, idleSince) for idle ones. ArrayDeque.removeAll { ... } throws out old ones, and removeLastOrNull() takes the newest.
A connection counts toward the maximum size whether it's in use or idle, so open is the size of the openedAt map, not of the idle deque.

drill.title: Write the retry decision from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write mayRetry(method, hasKey, outcome) for the outcomes refused, connect timeout, reset, read timeout and an HTTP status, and backoffMs(retry) with full jitter, a base of 100 ms and a cap of 2 s. Then put the idle timeouts of the pool, the load balancer and the backend in the order they must follow.

answer.html: fun isIdempotent(method: String, hasKey: Boolean) = method in setOf("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "TRACE", "PUT", "DELETE") || (method == "POST" && hasKey) fun mayRetry(method: String, hasKey: Boolean, outcome: Outcome): Boolean = when (outcome) { Outcome.ConnectRefused, Outcome.ConnectTimeout -> true // never sent Outcome.Reset, Outcome.ReadTimeout -> isIdempotent(method, hasKey) // maybe processed is Outcome.Status -> outcome.code in setOf(429, 502, 503, 504) && isIdempotent(method, hasKey) } fun backoffMs(retry: Int, random: () -> Double = Math::random): Long { val ceiling = minOf(2_000L, 100L shl (retry - 1).coerceAtMost(30)) // 100, 200, 400 ... 2,000 return (random() * ceiling).toLong() // anywhere below it } // Idle timeouts, shortest first: client pool < load balancer < backend server.

recap: A load balancer that acts as a proxy turns one request into two TCP connections. L4 picks a backend per connection and never reads HTTP. L7 ends TLS, reads every request, and routes each one over its own pool.
Backends behind a proxy see the proxy's address. The client's address travels in X-Forwarded-For (L7) or a PROXY protocol header (L4). Trust only the entries your own proxies added.

Every wait gets its own limit: a connection from the pool (milliseconds), the connect (a second or two), the answer (a little above the p99) and a deadline for the whole call. A limit on each read never catches a body that trickles in.

Retry only what is safe: anything never sent, and anything idempotent (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key). Wait random(0, min(cap, base x 2^n)), keep a retry budget, and retry at one layer.

Every hop forgets idle connections by its own clock (JDK client 30 s, AWS's L7 balancer 60 s, its L4 balancer and NAT gateways 350 s). Keep each client's idle timeout below the next hop's, or the first call after a quiet spell meets a reset.

The limit: none of this makes the network reliable. A request that was sent and got no answer still leaves the app not knowing what happened, and only an idempotency key, or asking the bank, settles it.

explain.prompt: A friend who looks after the café's payments app asks: "Every morning the first few payments after the quiet night fail with Connection reset, then everything is fine all day. The bank says its machines never saw those requests." Explain what is happening, and what you would change.
explain.answer: The app's pool keeps idle connections longer than something between the app and the bank does. Overnight the connections sit unused. The load balancer (or a NAT gateway) in front of the bank forgets them after its own idle timeout, 350 seconds for a network load balancer, and tells nobody. In the morning, the pool hands out one of those connections as if it were healthy. The request goes out, and the balancer, which no longer knows the connection, answers with a TCP reset. That's why the bank's machines never saw anything, and why it only happens after quiet spells. I'd set the pool's idle timeout below the balancer's, and add a maximum lifetime for each connection. I'd also allow one immediate retry on a fresh connection when a reused connection is reset before any answer, but only for idempotent requests, which for payments means sending an idempotency key. TCP keepalive probes sent more often than the balancer's timeout would also keep the connections alive.

deeper.html:
CDNs are caching L7 proxies. A CDN (content delivery network) is a fleet of L7 proxies close to users that keep copies of answers, following HTTP's caching rules (RFC 9111). Cache-Control: max-age says how long a copy stays fresh, Age how old it already is, and Vary which request headers change the answer. Most CDNs reach users through anycast, the same address announced from many places (lesson 4's Go deeper). For an API that moves money, almost nothing may be cached. A CDN still gives you TLS close to the user, and a long-lived pooled connection back to your own servers.

Choosing a backend. Taking turns (round robin) ignores how busy each backend is. "Least outstanding requests" sends each request to the backend with the fewest in flight, which copes better when some requests are slow. "Power of two choices" picks two backends at random and takes the less busy one, which is nearly as good and much cheaper to work out. Outlier detection takes a backend out as soon as it starts returning errors, without waiting for health checks to fail.

Hedged requests. For idempotent reads where a few answers are very slow, a client can send a second copy to another backend if the first hasn't answered by, say, the p95 (the time 95 answers in 100 beat), and use whichever answer comes first. The slowest answers get much faster for a few percent more load. Never hedge a payment.

When the request was sent but the answer never came. TCP_USER_TIMEOUT limits how long the kernel keeps resending unacknowledged data before it gives up on a connection. A read timeout doesn't do that if your code is busy writing, as Cloudflare's write-up of sockets that refuse to die explains. HTTP/2 PING frames can spot a dead connection without sending a request.
